steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Additive manufacturing builds components layer by layer from a digital model, adding material rather than removing it.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM) extrudes thermoplastic filament through a heated nozzle; the most common and affordable 3D printing method.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Selective Laser Sintering (SLS) uses a laser to fuse powdered material (nylon, metal) layer by layer; produces strong, functional parts.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Stereolithography (SLA) uses a UV laser to cure liquid resin; produces very high-resolution parts with smooth surface finish.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always name the specific additive process (FDM, SLS, SLA) rather than just writing '3D printing'. The key exam distinction: additive ADDS material, subtractive REMOVES material, forming SHAPES material. When evaluating additive vs traditional manufacturing, consider volume, complexity, material properties and cost. Anisotropy (layer weakness) is a common exam point: parts are weaker between layers than within them. Remember: no tooling costs is the main advantage for low-volume and prototype production.
